https://artdaily.com/news/199238/Aneta-K.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact Aneta Kajzer and Ilse Henin meet across generations in exhibition at Galerie Rupert Pfab Ilse Henin, ohne Titel, 100 x 70 cm, Pastellkreide auf Papier. DÜSSELDORF .- The paintings and drawings of Aneta Kajzer and Ilse Henin come together in face to face, an exhibition that places two artists from different generations in an unexpectedly close conversation. Opening September 4 and running through October 24, 2026, the show explores a shared fascination with transformation, nature and the increasingly fluid boundaries between human, animal and landscape. Despite the differences in their backgrounds and approaches, Kajzer and Henin create worlds in which identities rarely remain fixed. Bodies appear to merge with landscapes, organic forms suggest animals or faces, and figures seem to emerge only to dissolve again. Their works invite viewers into spaces where memory, imagination and lived experience overlap, and where distinctions between species and environments become less certain. For Aneta Kajzer, born in Katowice, Poland, in 1989, painting develops through an intuitive and highly responsive process. Her canvases often hover between abstraction and figuration, allowing forms to shift depending on how they are seen. A patch of color might suggest a landscape at first, then a face, an animal or an atmospheric event. That sense of instability is central to her work. Rather than guiding the viewer toward a single interpretation, Kajzer leaves her images deliberately open. Color plays an important role in that ambiguity, functioning not simply as a formal device but as a carrier of mood and narrative. In works such as In the Atmosphere from 2026, figures and environments seem to move in and out of one another. Landscapes can become bodies, while bodies appear to dissolve into weather or color. The result is a dreamlike world that feels both recognizable and strange. Kajzer has emerged as a notable voice in contemporary painting in Germany. She gained wider attention through her participation in JETZT! Junge Malerei in Deutschland in 2019 and 2020 and has received several awards, including a Stiftung Kunstfonds working grant, the Marianne Defet Painting Scholarship and the Kallmann Prize. Her work is represented in public collections including the German Federal Collection of Contemporary Art, Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz and FRAC Auvergne in France. Ilse Henin, born in Bad Godesberg in 1944, approaches many of the exhibition’s themes from a very different historical perspective. After studying at the Karlsruhe Academy of Fine Arts under Horst Egon Kalinowski from 1966 to 1970, she developed a distinctive visual language shaped by drawing, symbolism and an acute awareness of social and political change. Her artistic outlook was influenced by her childhood on a farm, extended stays in southern France and the political movements that reshaped Europe during the late 1960s and early 1970s. Feminism, environmental activism, the peace movement and the student protests of the period all formed part of the cultural landscape in which she worked. Yet Henin rarely addressed those concerns through straightforward political imagery. Instead, she created a poetic universe in which humans, animals and hybrid beings coexist on equal terms. Species boundaries become unstable, and transformation and interdependence emerge as recurring ideas. Seen today, those concerns can feel strikingly current. Henin’s work anticipated many of the questions now associated with ecological responsibility, feminism and posthumanist thinking, particularly the idea that human life cannot be understood separately from the larger natural systems surrounding it. Drawing remains at the center of her practice. Using economical and precise lines, Henin builds complex compositions that can feel simultaneously intimate and expansive. Color often enters as an atmospheric or emotional element, while the openness of her forms leaves room for multiple readings. Although Henin worked consistently for decades, her art remained relatively removed from mainstream art-historical attention for much of her career. That has begun to change. The 2023 exhibition Die unhintergehbare Verflechtung aller Leben at Kunsthalle Düsseldorf helped bring renewed attention to the relevance of her work and its relationship to contemporary conversations about climate, feminism and social change. Bringing Kajzer and Henin together highlights how artists separated by more than four decades can arrive at remarkably connected questions. One approaches them through the fluid language of contemporary painting, the other through a practice rooted in the political and ecological consciousness of the 1970s. In face to face, those differences become part of the exhibition’s strength. Rather than presenting a simple comparison between generations, the show suggests a longer continuity of artistic thinking about what it means to live among other beings—and how art can imagine a world in which the boundaries between people, animals and nature are far less fixed than they appear. face to face: Aneta Kajzer & Ilse Henin opens September 4, 2026, with an opening reception from 6 to 9 p.m. The exhibition continues through October 24. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Flushing a toilet can release particles into the air that remain suspended for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found. Photograph: Naruecha Jenthaisong/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Flushing a toilet can release particles into the air that remain suspended for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found. Photograph: Naruecha Jenthaisong/Getty Images Australia news Flushing the toilet can release a ‘plume’ of breathable pathogens – and closing the lid won’t stop their escape New research shows turbulent flushes create toilet-generated aerosols that can transmit legionella, influenza and norovirus Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tory Shepherd Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Flushing toilets release particles into the “breathing zone” of adults and can remain suspended in the air for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found. And closing the lid might not be enough to avoid a “plume” of potential pathogens. Meanwhile, previous research has shown public toilets are an inescapable hotbed of microbes. The perfect flush: eight essential toilet tips – from closed lids to cleaning Read more Flinders University researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, publishing the results in the Science of the Total Environment journal . They found microbes from the water used for flushing or from contamination of the bowl ended up as aerosols, with more “turbulent” flushing releasing more particles. That included bioaerosols – aerosols that contain biological material and can transmit pathogens including legionella, influenza and norovirus. There are differing reports about whether Covid spreads through toilet aerosols. The researchers found higher levels of aerosols in the water and higher levels of turbulence during the flush increased the volume of particles suspended in the air, but the effects of bathroom ventilation and whether the lid was up or down were unclear. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Despite that, lead author and PhD student Lira Adiyani said she would still recommend putting the lid down after using the toilet. “Toilet flushing creates turbulence that can release aerosols into the surrounding air,” she said. “Some studies detected these aerosols at adult breathing height, indicating a potential pathway for inhalation exposure. “The more microbes present in the toilet, the more bioaerosols may be released. Therefore, larger flush volumes generally produce more aerosols.” Adiyani said “based on the available evidence” she would still recommend closing the lid as a precautionary measure, “while recognising that it does not completely prevent aerosols from escaping”. In the report, the researchers wrote that the effects of indoor aerosols had been “understudied” despite the risk of infection. This had “important implications for risk assessment, building design, and infection control in an era of water security pressures and emerging infectious diseases”, they wrote. “Indoor aerosols influence air quality and human health as their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory tract when inhaled, providing a direct exposure pathway.” Co-author, environmental health professor Harriet Whiley, said people didn’t have to be worried in their own homes, unless someone in the house was immunocompromised. She said the team was working on “protecting the most vulnerable through good design” in places such as hospitals and aged care environments. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion They are increasingly concerned about “opportunistic pathogens” that can be present in water, particularly recycled or rainwater. “They don’t affect healthy people,” she said. “But if you’re immunocompromised you can get very sick, and it can be fatal.” So it’s about getting “an effective flush with less volume and less turbulence”, she said. Dr Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular genetics at Bond and Murdoch universities wasn’t involved in the research but warned bathroom dangers go well beyond the toilet. His own research is particularly focused on public toilets and mobile phone use in toilets. “As soon as you enter a toilet, consider everything contaminated,” he said. The door will have microbes on it, as will the floor – so you should never put anything on it, he said. Then you might touch the lid, after which you flush with the lid up or down. If it’s up, you get the “plume” effect, an “explosion or aerosols … you are literally sprayed [with]”. Flushing with the lid down might limit your exposure to the plume, but depending on the cleanliness of the toilet, previous users have left microorganisms on every surface anyway. “The roof, the walls, the floor,” he said. Then, you touch the toilet door again, before (hopefully) washing your hands. But you will probably touch the taps again, blow microorganisms around with the hairdryer, touch the exit door and then touch your phone. “Studies show between 50% and 80% of people use mobile phones in the toilet. For younger generations it’s almost 100%,” he said. “They will contaminate their phones and fingers with fecal microorganisms – salmonella, campylobacter, all sorts of bacteria and viruses. “The less contact you have, the better it is.” Explore more on these topics Australia news Microbiology Infectious diseases Health Hygiene news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Supporters of Pakistan’s PTI party take part in a protest march demanding Imran Khan's release from prison. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Supporters of Pakistan’s PTI party take part in a protest march demanding Imran Khan's release from prison. Photograph: Reuters Pakistan Imran Khan’s party decries ‘coup’ after Pakistan suspends provincial government Suspension of provincial government escalates standoff with Khan’s PTI party a week after his supporters began marching to demand his release Reuters Sun 11 Oct 2026 20.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province ⁠led by Imran ​Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”. President Asif Ali Zardari ​declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan. The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between ⁠Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release. Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in ​what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years. Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest. Supporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down Islamabad Read more Pakistan’s constitution ‌allows the government to take over from ‌provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number ‌of militant attacks in recent months. Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province. The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs. Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters. Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father Read more Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad. In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament. Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats ⁠in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say ​the military rigged the vote against him, which the ​military denies. Cases against Khan range from concerns over state ​gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, ​with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing. President Zardari ​declared the emergency on the advice of ​the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said. Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.” Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.
